title: Seven years of runway against the CPO timing
body:
## The arithmetic of patience

The most unusual feature of POET Technologies at the snapshot date was not its technology, its board, or its binary market position. It was the time it had purchased.

The company closed fiscal year 2025 with $313.4 million in cash and short-term investments against an annualised cash operating loss of approximately $45 million — the gap between a $62.96 million net loss and roughly $18 million in non-cash charges including stock-based compensation, depreciation and amortisation. At that burn rate, POET carried approximately seven years of runway. For a pre-commercial-revenue company navigating an architectural transition in a market where even the largest hyperscalers had not yet committed publicly to co-packaged optics volume timelines, seven years was a structurally long position. It was not infinite, but it was long enough to outlast several cycles of industry uncertainty.

The runway was manufactured in a single transaction. POET's $250 million institutional equity raise — three buyers, none publicly named at the snapshot date — expanded the balance sheet from $69.7 million at December 2024 to $328.6 million at December 2025, a near-fivefold expansion in twelve months. [POET Technologies Q4 2025 financial results](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-reports-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results) The three institutions that funded that transaction effectively made a calculation: the CPO transition would take longer than the market priced, and a company with the right architecture and the right board composition would be worth holding through the uncertainty. The seven-year runway was the price of that bet.

## The catalyst sequence

Against that runway, POET's forward value was entirely sequenced around external events it could not control.

The nearest-term catalyst was the quarterly 6-K cadence through 2026. POET's fiscal 2025 produced approximately $1.2 million in non-recurring engineering and small product receipts — a revenue line that did not cover a single quarter of the $18.08 million R&D budget. [POET Technologies 20-F annual report](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/POET/20-f-poet-technologies-inc-files-annual-report-foreign-issuer-eeda6513f179.html) The investment community tracking the stock would parse each successive quarterly filing for evidence that NRE revenues were progressing toward qualification milestones — the specific signal that one or more hyperscaler engineering teams had advanced the Optical Interposer from evaluation through to design-in, the penultimate step before volume purchase orders.

The September 2025 Sivers Semiconductors collaboration established the template for what a meaningful interim partnership announcement could look like. Sivers Photonics, the UK subsidiary of Swedish listed Sivers Semiconductors, designed high-power indium phosphide distributed-feedback lasers; POET's Optical Interposer provided the wafer-level integration substrate to combine those lasers with modulators, photodetectors and filters in a single external light source module. [POET and Sivers collaboration](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) The pairing positioned two pre-revenue platform companies as complementary upstream components for hyperscaler CPO supply chains. Additional partnerships of that character — with laser suppliers, DSP developers, or packaging houses — would represent the same category of signal: the supply chain for a POET-enabled CPO module was being assembled, even if no hyperscaler had yet signed a volume agreement.

The medium-term catalyst sequence ran through 2027. Broadcom's Tomahawk CPO programme was the most consequential demand-side datapoint in the sector; Tomahawk 5 CPO-enabled switch ASICs were the most concrete shipped evidence that at least one major merchant-silicon vendor had committed engineering resources to the co-packaged architecture. How aggressively Broadcom's hyperscaler customers specified CPO configurations in their 2026 and 2027 purchasing — and which optical-engine suppliers they qualified — would determine whether the CPO ramp was a 2027 event or a 2029 event. Nvidia's Rubin architecture disclosures, expected in the late 2026 to 2027 timeframe, carried similar weight: Nvidia's choice of optical interconnect architecture for next-generation GPU clusters would either validate or complicate the case for CPO at the AI-training layer, which was increasingly the highest-density interconnect environment in the industry.

## The binary architecture

The investment outcome was structurally binary in a way that defied conventional valuation frameworks.

Scenario A: CPO adoption at hyperscale proceeded on the faster-than-consensus trajectory, and POET's Optical Interposer was qualified as a component in one or more of those supply chains. Under that outcome, the revenue ramp from a single hyperscaler design win at modest volume could plausibly reach $200 million or more in annual revenue by 2028 or 2029 — a number that would represent more than 150 times the company's fiscal 2025 revenue figure. Gross-margin parity with vertically integrated photonics peers like Coherent or Lumentum — companies that operated at 30 to 40 percent gross margins on manufacturing-volume photonics — was conceivable at that revenue scale, given that the Optical Interposer's wafer-level integration approach was specifically engineered to reduce assembly and alignment costs relative to component-by-component packaging. At $500 million or more in annual revenue — an aggressive 2029-to-2030 figure contingent on qualification at multiple hyperscalers — POET would approach cash-flow breakeven, and the economic significance of the 37.36 million warrants outstanding would diminish relative to share-price appreciation. The $135.6 million derivative warrant liability, one of the most consequential single line items on the balance sheet at the snapshot date, would become a manageable dilution event rather than an overhang.

Scenario B: Pluggable optics continued to dominate the addressable market. Applied Optoelectronics, Coherent, and Lumentum — vertically integrated transceiver manufacturers with existing customer relationships, qualified production lines, and revenue bases that dwarfed POET's — captured the volume that CPO proponents expected to transition off pluggable architectures. Under that outcome, each year of POET's runway was a year of burn against a thesis that was not crystallising. At seven years of runway, the company had time to watch two full hyperscaler hardware-refresh cycles pass before running out of capital — but watching those cycles pass without a design win would compress the optionality value progressively. By year five without commercial revenue, the market would almost certainly have re-rated the equity toward liquidation value, which at the snapshot date was roughly $313.4 million in cash plus whatever residual IP value an acquirer ascribed to the Optical Interposer platform.

| Scenario | Revenue trajectory | Cash-flow inflection | Dilution outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPO wins, POET qualified | $200M+ by 2028-29 (one hyperscaler) | Positive by $500M+ (2029-30) | Warrants dilutive but absorbed by appreciation |
| Pluggable dominates | Runway consumed without thesis | No inflection within runway | Warrants remain full economic overhang |

## The acquisition overhang

A third scenario sat implicitly behind both of the above: acquisition before the binary resolved.

POET at $313.4 million in cash with a validated Optical Interposer platform would have been an unusual asset on several acquirer balance sheets. Intel's silicon photonics organisation had been a long-running internal programme without a clear path to leading the CPO transition from within; an external interposer platform with a Singapore-based wafer-level integration line would have filled a gap. Marvell, which had built its optical networking position through the Inphi acquisition and subsequent optical engine investments, carried structural incentives to extend that platform upstream toward the laser-and-integration layer. Broadcom, already shipping Tomahawk CPO silicon and managing its optical-engine supply chain, had a vertical-integration motive to insource a component that was currently supplied by third parties. Coherent, as a vertically integrated photonics company with both InP laser and silicon photonics lines, could have absorbed the POET platform to add wafer-level interposer capability without building it organically.

No public signal of any such transaction existed at the snapshot date. But the board composition carried pattern recognition that was not accidental. Jean-Louis Malinge had run Kotura through to its sale to Mellanox in 2013 — a transaction that converted a silicon photonics platform company into an acquired subsidiary of what eventually became part of NVIDIA's networking stack. Sohail Khan, the most recent board addition as of July 2025, had served as CEO of Agere Systems through an extended period of M&A activity before the company's eventual acquisition by LSI Logic. Together with Suresh Venkatesan's background navigating the GlobalFoundries-Samsung technology-licensing environment, the board had accumulated more transaction-execution experience than most pre-revenue companies of POET's size were assembled with. That composition was not sufficient evidence of intent, but it was not evidence of inexperience either.

## The question the runway was built to answer

What the $250 million institutional raise, the Sivers collaboration, the Singapore fabrication line, and the seven-year cash runway collectively constructed was not a business in the ordinary sense. It was a structured bet on a question that the semiconductor industry had not yet resolved at the snapshot date: whether the co-packaged optics architectural transition would proceed fast enough, and consistently enough across hyperscaler purchasing decisions, to create a qualified supply-chain position for a wafer-level photonic integration platform before competing architectures — monolithic silicon photonics, pluggable 200G lanes, or next-generation VCSEL arrays — locked the market into a different technical consensus.

POET's Optical Interposer had a credible answer to that question on paper. The wafer-level integration approach addressed the assembly-cost problem that had historically made photonic integration expensive at scale. The Singapore manufacturing base provided geographic insulation from US export-control exposure. The board carried the operational vocabulary to govern through a qualification-and-volume ramp if one materialised. And the seven-year runway provided the temporal buffer to wait for the hyperscaler community to make its architectural choices visible through purchasing behaviour rather than roadmap presentations.

Whether that was enough — whether seven years purchased enough time for CPO to crystallise, and whether POET's interposer was one of the components the hyperscalers chose to crystallise it around — was precisely the question the report had been built to frame. The cash was real. The architecture was coherent. The runway was long. The answer was not yet in.
